title: GTA VI Just Made $4 Billion in Four Days—and Broke the Entire Entertainment Industry
excerpt: Thirteen years of hype, two delays, and a $79.99 price tag didn't slow Rockstar down. Grand Theft Auto VI just out-earned Hollywood's biggest blockbusters in a single weekend.
pullQuote: In 24 hours, GTA VI beat the entire lifetime box office of Avengers: Endgame.
body: Grand Theft Auto VI—Rockstar Games' massive open-world crime epic set in the Florida-inspired state of Leonida—finally dropped on November 19, 2026. After a 13-year wait since GTA V and two high-profile delays, it didn't just meet the hype; it vaporized every sales record in entertainment history.

According to Take-Two Interactive, the game pulled in $3.79 billion in retail sales on day one alone. That is nearly five times GTA V's $800 million debut in 2013, and more than Avengers: Endgame made across its entire theatrical run.

By the end of its four-day launch weekend, analytics firm Alinea estimated sales had hit 44.9 million copies and crossed $4 billion in gross revenue. PlayStation 5 dominated the rush, accounting for 75.1% of sales (33.7 million copies) compared to Xbox's 11.2 million.

Why did it explode? Pent-up demand did the heavy lifting, backed by a decade of GTA Online keeping the franchise culturally unavoidable. Add in a $79.99 standard price tag—and legions of fans shelling out $99.99 for the Ultimate Edition—and Rockstar turned a video game launch into a global financial event.

Critics are just as swept up as the buyers. The game debuted with a 99 out of 100 average on Metacritic, with outlets like The Guardian already calling it "the greatest game ever made" for its obsessive world detail and sheer scale.

Still, the launch wasn't glitch-free. The day-one surge triggered PlayStation Network outages, players have reported save-wiping crashes, and despite generating billions in a weekend, reports indicate Rockstar developers are still bracing for post-launch layoffs—a grim reminder of how the modern games industry actually works.

title: No, Google’s New AI Didn’t Just Crack RSA Encryption—Here’s What Actually Happened
excerpt: Google’s multi-agent AI just dropped six autonomous math papers and sent crypto Twitter into a spiral. The reality is impressive, but your passwords are fine.
pullQuote: The algorithm is a theoretical win, not a skeleton key—it’s actually slower than methods we already use.
body: On November 25, Google published six mathematical research papers generated by Cogentic, a multi-agent AI system built on Gemini 4. According to Google, the system produced the proofs without human intervention beyond the initial prompt.

One manuscript immediately set off alarm bells across the internet: "Unconditional Integer Factorization in Time L_N[1/3, O(1)]." Because integer factorization is the math locking down RSA encryption and much of the web, rumors of an imminent crypto meltdown spread fast.

Here is the reality check. While the paper describes a classical algorithm that factors integers without relying on unproven mathematical hypotheses, it is a purely theoretical upgrade—not a practical weapon.

The new method is still considerably slower than existing factorization techniques and does not solve the problem in polynomial time. Modern RSA encryption and Bitcoin security face zero immediate threat from it.

The other five papers tackle heavy computer science problems like discrete logarithms, approximate Nash equilibria, and graph reconstruction. It is a major flex for autonomous AI reasoning, even if experts warn that partial machine-checked proofs still need full independent validation.
The real headline isn't that AI broke the internet's locks. It's that AI is now writing publishable theoretical math on its own—and the internet is still terrible at reading past the abstract.
